Rajma Chawal, the way my dadi used to make it

Posted by Meera K. · 14 min read · Filed under: Rajasthani comfort food

Every family in Jaipur seems to have its own rajma recipe, and everyone is absolutely certain theirs is the correct one. Mine comes from my grandmother, who insisted the secretly delicious part of the dish was never the spices but the soaking time - a full night, no exceptions, no matter how late you got home from work.

Start with 250g of dried kidney beans, rinsed and soaked overnight in plenty of water. The next day, drain them and set them aside while you build the base: two finely chopped onions, four cloves of garlic, an inch of ginger, and three tomatoes blended into a smooth puree.

Heat ghee in a heavy-bottomed pot - this is non-negotiable in my house. Butter can work in a pinch and acts as a reasonable substitute for flavor, but ghee handles the long simmer without burning the way butter sometimes does. Add cumin seeds and let them crackle before the onions go in.

Cook the onions until they're properly golden, not just translucent - this takes longer than most recipes admit, usually a full twelve minutes on medium heat. Add the garlic and ginger, cook for another minute, then the tomato puree, and let the whole thing reduce until the oil starts to separate at the edges of the pot.

Now the spices: turmeric, red chili powder, coriander powder, and a good pinch of garam masala saved for the very end. Add the soaked rajma along with fresh water, bring it to a boil, then let it simmer - covered, low heat - for at least an hour. A pressure cooker gets you there in twenty minutes if you're short on time, but the stovetop version has a better texture in my opinion.

Finish with a final sprinkle of garam masala and a generous handful of chopped coriander. Serve over steamed basmati rice with a wedge of lemon and, if you have it, a spoon of ghee melted right on top of the rice before the rajma goes on.

Comments (3)

Priya S.: Made this last weekend and my kitchen smelled exactly like my nani's. The overnight soak really does make a difference, I used to skip that step and regret it every time.

Arjun T.: Tried swapping the ghee for mustard oil at the start just to see - it changes the flavor completely, not better or worse, just different. Worth trying once.

Deepa M.: Question - does this freeze well? I usually make a double batch on Sundays for the week.
